title: DbContext lifetime (scoped per request, thread safety)
hook: DbContext is not thread-safe and must not live longer than one unit of work. In ASP.NET Core Web APIs it is scoped — one instance per HTTP request, disposed when the response completes.

blocks.text: DbContext lifetime determines how long EF Core keeps a database connection, change tracker, and cached metadata alive. AddDbContext<T>() registers DbContext as scoped by default — the dependency injection (DI) container creates one instance per HTTP request scope and disposes it when the request ends. DbContext is explicitly not thread-safe: two parallel tasks must not share the same instance. Background services (singletons) must use IServiceScopeFactory to create a fresh scope — and DbContext — per work item.

entries.plainDefinition: One instance per DI scope. In web apps, one scope per HTTP request.
A single consistent boundary for queries and SaveChanges — typically one DbContext per request.
entries.example: Multiple repository calls in one handler share the same DbContext and transaction.

entries.plainDefinition: DbContext cannot be used concurrently from multiple threads or overlapping async operations.
entries.example: InvalidOperationException: A second operation was started on this context...

entries.plainDefinition: Factory to create DI scopes from singleton services — required for background DbContext usage.

blocks.text: Wrong DbContext lifetime causes cross-request data leaks, memory growth, and concurrency exceptions. Singleton DbContext is the fastest rejection in senior interviews. Parallel foreach over one DbContext triggers 'second operation on this context'. Captive dependency — singleton holding scoped DbContext — is the #1 EF production bug. Monitoring ActiveDbContexts in production proves whether lifetimes are correct.

blocks.title: Microsoft guidance
blocks.body: Do not make DbContext singleton. Do not share one DbContext instance across threads. Do not inject DbContext into singleton services — use IServiceScopeFactory instead.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Request arrives
items.body: ASP.NET Core creates an IServiceScope from the root provider.

items.title: DbContext resolved
items.body: First injection of AppDbContext creates the instance with pooled DbContextOptions.

items.title: Handler uses context
items.body: All services in the same request share the identical DbContext instance.

items.title: SaveChanges (optional)
items.body: Pending changes flush to the database within this context's connection.

items.title: Scope disposed
items.body: DbContext.Dispose() returns connection to pool; change tracker cleared.

snippet.label: Correct scoped registration and injection
snippet.explanation: AddDbContext registers scoped. Handler and OrderService in the same request share one DbContext. Never register AddSingleton<AppDbContext>().

snippet.label: Background work with IServiceScopeFactory
snippet.explanation: BackgroundService is singleton. CreateAsyncScope per batch gives a fresh scoped DbContext. Scope disposal releases the context even if an exception occurs.

snippet.label: Thread-safety violation — never do this
snippet.explanation: DbContext allows only one active operation at a time. Parallel.ForEachAsync on shared context throws. Batch updates in one context sequentially, or use a scope per parallel partition.

snippet.label: Diagnostics — ActiveDbContexts counter
snippet.explanation: ActiveDbContexts stuck at 1 under concurrent load proves singleton or captive scoped DbContext. Load test with k6; watch for ObjectDisposedException and second-operation errors.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Registering DbContext as singleton for 'performance'. Injecting AppDbContext into singleton cache warmer or middleware constructor. Using Task.WhenAll on multiple queries against one DbContext. Creating manual new AppDbContext() instead of DI — bypasses pooling and scope disposal. Storing DbContext in static fields.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore — ActiveDbContexts tracks live contexts. Under steady load it should track concurrent requests, not grow unbounded. OpenTelemetry spans with overlapping database operations on the same trace from different requests indicate shared context. Enable ValidateScopes in CI — singleton resolving scoped DbContext from root provider fails at startup. Load test reveals ObjectDisposedException when captive dependencies surface under concurrency.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Multiple contexts per request — no shared transaction
Thread safety, stale tracker, memory leak
Options are singleton; context instance still scoped
Caller must dispose; not automatic per request

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying DbContext can be singleton 'because connections are pooled' — pooling is on DbContextOptions, not the context instance. Not knowing DbContext is not thread-safe. Unable to explain IServiceScopeFactory for BackgroundService. Dismissing ValidateScopes warnings.

interviewTakeaways: DbContext is scoped per request, not thread-safe, disposed at scope end — AddDbContext registers scoped by default.
When not to share: parallel tasks, singleton services, background workers without CreateScope.
Production tip: dotnet-counters ActiveDbContexts ≈ concurrent requests; ValidateScopes in CI; IServiceScopeFactory in BackgroundService.

60s: DbContext scoped per HTTP request. Not thread-safe — one operation at a time. Singleton services use IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope per work item. ActiveDbContexts stuck at 1 means captive dependency. Never singleton DbContext.
Follow-up: when would you use IDbContextFactory instead of injected DbContext?
commonPitfalls: Singleton DbContext 'for connection pooling' gets rejected — pooling is on options; context holds tracker and is not thread-safe.
Parallel.WhenAll on one DbContext — InvalidOperationException in production under load.
Strong answer: 'Scoped per request via DI. Background work uses IServiceScopeFactory per message. Monitor ActiveDbContexts. DbContext is unit-of-work, not a connection wrapper — never singleton.'
introducedIn: EF Core 1.0; DbContext pooling in EF Core 2.0

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeORM EntityManager with Scope.REQUEST mirrors scoped DbContext — one manager per HTTP request, disposed after response. Injecting into singleton throws, same as ValidateScopes.
Prisma uses a singleton client with internal connection pool — different from EF's per-request DbContext. Node developers must not assume Prisma's pattern applies to DbContext lifetime.
